summary: Presents user requirements for SIP to support deaf, hard of hearing and speech-impaired people. It describes the difficulties these users face with communication tools today, and the opportunities SIP-based communication offers for text, video and other media.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3351 lists what the Session Initiation Protocol, or SIP, would need to do for deaf, hard of hearing and speech-impaired people to use it properly. It describes the problems these users have today, sets out six requirements, and then walks through real situations such as a relay service turning speech into text during a call.

subtitle: What the Session Initiation Protocol would have to do so deaf, hard of hearing and speech-impaired people can use it

tldr.problem: Communication devices built for deaf, hard of hearing and speech-impaired people are often primitive, expensive and unable to talk to each other, and the services that let these people reach the telephone network are mostly staffed by people working by hand.
tldr.mechanism: The memo states six user requirements for SIP, covering easy connection, a user profile that says how a person wants to communicate, gateways to legacy equipment, inclusive design, resource management by the user agent, and confidentiality of everything a third party handles.
tldr.outcome: SIP can hold several media streams at once and swap them during a call, so a relay or transcoding service can carry speech as text and a signing avatar can be added to a call. The memo is a statement of requirements and worked examples, not a protocol or a specification.

today: RFC 3351 is an Informational memo from August 2002 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It states user requirements and worked examples for SIP in support of deaf, hard of hearing and speech-impaired people, and it says so explicitly that it is not meant to penalise other users.

sections.title: The Terms This Memo Uses
sections.content:
The memo defines its own vocabulary. Abilities are a person's capacity for communicating, which could include a hearing or speech impairment or not. Preferences are a person's choice of communication mode, which could include any combination of media streams, such as text, audio or video. Both terms apply to the caller and to the person receiving the call.

A relay service is a third party or intermediary that enables communications between deaf, hard of hearing and speech-impaired people, and people without a hearing or speech impairment. Relay services form a subset of the activities of transcoding services, where a transcoding service is a human or automated third party that acts as an intermediary in any session between two other user agents, being a user agent itself, and transcodes one stream into another, for example voice to text or the reverse.

A textphone, sometimes called a TTY, a TDD or a minicom, enables a deaf, hard of hearing or speech-impaired person to place a call to a telephone or another textphone. Some textphones use the V.18 protocol as a standard for communication with other textphone communication protocols worldwide. A user, throughout the document, is a deaf, hard of hearing or speech-impaired individual.

The memo notes that a deaf, hard of hearing or speech-impaired person here is an individual who chooses to use SIP because it can minimise or eliminate constraints in using common communication devices. As SIP promises a total communication solution for any kind of person, regardless of ability and preference, there is no attempt to specifically define deaf, hard of hearing or speech-impaired in the document.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo separates what a person can do from what a person would prefer to use, for example text rather than speech. It then names the two kinds of helper: a relay service, and a transcoding service that converts one kind of stream into another.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
The scope is first to present a current set of user requirements for deaf, hard of hearing and speech-impaired individuals through SIP-enabled communications. These are followed by real world scenarios in SIP communications that could be used in a test environment, and some concepts of how these requirements can be developed by service providers and user agent manufacturers.

The recommendations make explicit the needs of a currently often disadvantaged user group and attempt to match them with the capacity of SIP. It is not the intention to prioritise the needs of deaf, hard of hearing and speech-impaired people in a way that would penalise other individuals. The requirements aim to encourage developers and manufacturers worldwide to consider the specific needs of these people, and the document presents a world-view where deafness, hard of hearing or speech impairment are no longer a barrier to communication.

The background is the recent development of SIP and SIP-based communications, and a growing awareness of deaf, hard of hearing and speech-impaired issues in the technical community. The capacity of SIP to simplify setting up, managing and tearing down communication sessions between all kinds of user agents has specific implications for these individuals. As SIP enables multiple sessions with translation between multiple types of media, the requirements aim to provide the standard for recognising and enabling these interactions, and for a communications model that includes any and all types of SIP-networking abilities and preferences.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a list of what users need, plus examples, not a protocol. The authors are asking makers of phones, software and services to build for people whose communication needs differ from the average.

sections.title: Why These Requirements
sections.content:
Deaf, hard of hearing and speech-impaired people are currently often unable to use commonly available communication devices. Although this is documented, that does not mean that developers or manufacturers are always aware of it. Communication devices for these people are currently often primitive in design, expensive, and non-compatible with progressively designed, cheaper and more adaptable communication devices for other individuals. For example, many models of textphone are unable to communicate with other models.

Additionally, non-technical human communications, for example sign languages or lip-reading, are non-standard around the world.

There are intermediary or third-party relay services, for example transcoding services, that facilitate communications, uni- or bi-directional, for deaf, hard of hearing and speech-impaired people. Currently relay services are mostly operator-assisted, that is, manual, although methods of partial automation are being implemented in some areas. These services enable full access to modern facilities and conveniences, and although they are somewhat limited, their value is undeniable compared with their previous complete unavailability.

Yet communication methods in recent decades have proliferated: e-mail, mobile phones, video streaming. These methods are an advance in the development of data transfer technologies between devices. Developers and advocates of SIP agree that it is a protocol that not only anticipates the growth in real-time communications between convergent networks, but also fulfils the potential of the Internet as a communications and information forum, and that these developments allow a standard of communication that can be applied throughout all networking communities, regardless of abilities and preferences.
sections.plainLanguage: The problem is not that the technology is missing, but that the devices built for these users are old-fashioned and cannot talk to each other. Relay services that connect them to the ordinary telephone network exist, but today most of them are staffed by people doing the translating by hand.

sections.title: The Six Requirements for SIP
sections.content:
Connection without difficulty: whatever the preferences and abilities of the user and user agent, there should be no difficulty in setting up SIP sessions. These sessions could include multiple proxies, call routing decisions, transcoding services such as the relay service Typetalk or other media processing, and could include multiple simultaneous or alternative media streams. This means that any user agent in the conversation, including transcoding services, must be able to add or remove a media stream from the call without having to tear it down and re-establish it.

User profile: deaf, hard of hearing and speech-impaired user abilities and preferences must be communicable by SIP, and those abilities and preferences must determine the handling of the session. The profile might include how media streams are received and transmitted, such as text, voice or video, uni- or bi-directional; redirecting specific media streams through a transcoding service; roaming, for example a deaf person accessing their profile from a web interface at an Internet cafe; and anonymity, meaning not revealing that a deaf person is calling, even through a transcoding service. Part of this requirement is to ensure that these people can keep their preferences and abilities confidential, to avoid possible discrimination or prejudice, while still being able to establish a SIP session.

Intelligent gateways: SIP should support a class of user agents that perform as gateways for legacy systems designed for deaf, hard of hearing and speech-impaired people, for example a SIP user agent acting as a gateway to a public switched telephone network legacy textphone. Inclusive design: design concepts for communications must include the abilities and preferences of deaf, hard of hearing and speech-impaired people, and transcoding services and user agents must be able to connect with each other regardless of provider or manufacturer. That means new user agents must be able to support legacy protocols through appropriate gateways.

Resource management: user agents should be able to identify the content of a media stream in order to obtain information such as the cost of the media stream, and should be able to choose among transcoding services based on their capabilities and on any policy constraints they impose, such as charging for use. It should be possible for user agents to discover the availability of alternative media streams and choose from them.

Confidentiality and security: all third parties or intermediaries employed in a session for deaf, hard of hearing and speech-impaired people must offer a confidentiality policy, and all information exchanged in this type of session should be secure, that is, erased before confidentiality is breached, unless otherwise required. Transcoding services, such as interpretation and translation, must publish their confidentiality and security policies.
sections.plainLanguage: The six requirements say: a call should be easy to start whatever the user needs; the user's needs should travel with them in a profile that can stay private; old textphones should be reachable through a gateway; devices should be designed for everyone; the user's own software should choose services and see what they cost; and any third party in the call must publish a confidentiality policy and erase what it handles.

sections.title: Real World Scenarios
sections.content:
The scenarios show the kinds of media streams that would be initiated, managed, directed and terminated in a SIP-enabled network, and how resources might be managed between SIP-enabled networks, transcoding services and service providers.

In the transcoding service scenario, a hearing person calls the household of a deaf person and a hearing person. A voice conversation starts between the hearing participants. During the conversation the hearing person asks to talk with the deaf person, keeping the voice connection open so that voice to voice communication can continue if required. A relay service is invited into the conversation and transcodes the hearing person's words into text. The text appears on the display of the deaf person's user agent, who types a response. The relay service receives the text and reads it to the hearing person. When the hearing person asks to talk with the other hearing person in the deaf person's household, the relay service withdraws from the call.

In the media service provider scenario, a deaf person wants the content of a radio program as a text stream transcoded from the audio stream. The user's agent asks the radio station whether a text stream is available. If the station has none and says so, the deaf person's user agent requests a voice-to-text transcoding service, but that service's policy is that it does not accept radio broadcasts because it would overload its resources far too quickly, so the connection fails. The alternative is that the radio station does provide text with its audio streams, and the deaf person receives a text stream of the radio program. The memo notes that service providers are encouraged to provide text with audio streams.

The other scenarios cover a sign language interface, where a signing avatar is driven by XML data; synthetic lip-speaking support for voice calls, where software on a PC displays an animated face a hard of hearing person may be able to lip-read; voice-activated menu systems, where a textphone user books cinema tickets with a credit card through a relay service; and a conference call between five people, each with a different ability and preference, which needs four intermediate transcoding services. Where no direct speech-to-sign translation existed, the memo used a chain of intermediate services instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The worked examples show how a relay service turns speech into text mid-call and then leaves when it is no longer needed, why a radio station that offers no text stream may leave a deaf listener with no service at all, and how a five-person conference call with five different needs needs four translation services chained together.

sections.title: What the Memo Suggests to Builders
sections.content:
The memo suggests that service providers and user agent manufacturers offer a deaf, hard of hearing or speech-impaired person the possibility of preventing their specific abilities and preferences from being made public in any transaction. If a user agent performs auditory signalling, for example a pager, it could also provide another signalling method, visual such as a flashing light or tactile such as vibration. Service providers who let the user store abilities and preferences might consider storing these settings in a central repository, accessible no matter where the user is and regardless of the user agent used at that time.

If several transcoding services are available, the user agent can be set to select the most economical or highest quality service. The service provider can show the cost per minute and any minimum charge of a transcoding service call before a session starts, so the user can choose whether to use it. Service providers are encouraged to offer an alternative stream to an audio stream, for example text or data streams that operate avatars, and to provide a text alternative to voice-activated menus, answering and voice mail systems. Manufacturers of voice-activated software are encouraged to provide an alternative visual format for software prompts, menus, messages and status information, and manufacturers of mobile phones are encouraged to design equipment that avoids electro-magnetic interference with hearing aids.

All services for interpreting, transliterating or facilitating communications for these people are required to keep information exchanged during the transaction strictly confidential, to enable information exchange literally and simply without deviating from and compromising the content, to facilitate communication without bias, prejudice or opinion, to match skill sets to the requirements of the users of the service, to behave in a professional and appropriate manner, to be fair in pricing, and to strive to improve the skill sets used for their services. Conference call services might consider ways to let users who employ transcoding services, which usually introduce a delay, have real-time information sufficient to identify gaps in the conversation so they could inject comments, and ways to raise their hand, vote and carry out other activities where the timing of their response relative to the real-time conversation is important.
sections.plainLanguage: The suggestions are practical: a second way to signal, a profile stored where any device can reach it, the cost of a relay service shown before the call, and rules that every interpreting service must follow.

items.title: Connection without difficulty
items.text: Streams can be added or removed during a call without tearing it down

items.title: User profile
items.text: Abilities and preferences travel with the user and can stay private

items.title: Intelligent gateways
items.text: A SIP user agent can act as a gateway to a legacy textphone

items.title: Inclusive design
items.text: Devices and services are built for all abilities and work with each other

items.title: Resource management
items.text: The user agent can find services, compare them and see what they cost

items.title: Confidentiality and security
items.text: Every third party in the call publishes a policy and erases what it handles
